To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the climate of the present (∼2000) interglacial is ∼2–4 K warmer than it would have been without the anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions of early agriculture and the industrial era, and (2) the area of year-round ice cover is larger than it would have otherwise been.
the climate would be ∼2.7 K colder without the combined anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing of both early agriculture and industrial era, with the ocean playing an important amplification role.
the current interglaciation is warmer than previous interglaciations, and that the climate model results suggest that early agriculture may have caused some of this warming.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the hypothesis that early human agricultural activities caused a large increase in atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, which in turn caused the climate warming that has occurred over the past 10,000 years.
the question of how much the climate would have changed if greenhouse gases had remained at their low natural levels.
the role of early agricultural emissions in the current inter-glacial warming and in the absence of industrial era emissions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the early anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing was sufficient to cause the observed climate warming, but that ocean feedbacks may have amplified the warming.
the climate would be colder without the combined anthropogenic greenhouse forcing of the early agricultural and industrial eras, but the magnitude of this change is still uncertain.
the climate would have been much colder without the combined effects of the early agriculture and industrial eras.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the early agricultural hypothesis, if valid, would have been a major factor in the initiation of the modern interglacial and that it is possible that natural ocean feedback mechanisms could have contributed to the additional CO2 increase beyond the level attributed directly to early agriculture.
early agriculture, with its attendant increases of greenhouse gases, may have initiated the current interglaciation, and that the resulting warming may have caused the onset of the current ice age.

the hypothesis that the current interglacials are warmer than previous interglacialis due to anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions is consistent with observations, with model simulations of the early agriculture period, and with model estimates of natural ocean feedbacks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the climate system, including the ocean, is sensitive to greenhouse gas changes, even when these changes are modest.
the current climate is warmer than would otherwise exist without anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions.
the climate system is very sensitive to greenhouse gas forcing.
